screens.title: Introduction to C# and Unity Scripting Basics
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome to the practical introduction to C# in Unity. In this lesson you will learn why C# is the standard language for Unity scripting, how Unity uses classes that inherit from MonoBehaviour to run game behavior, and the basic lifecycle events that determine when your code executes. You will see a small set of essential patterns: creating a C# script file, matching the class name to the filename, attaching that script as a component to a GameObject, and using the print-style Debug. Log function to observe runtime behavior in the Unity Console. Understanding these ideas early saves time when you begin building interactions like player movement, simple AI, or UI responses. A concrete example you will practice is making a Hello World logger that prints messages when the script wakes and when the game starts. Along the way we will highlight two common pitfalls: mismatched filenames and unattached scripts, and the performance cost of logging every frame. By the end of this chapter you will know how to get a simple script running in the Editor and how to reason about what runs when. Ready to begin exploring the core topics and hands-on steps that follow?

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Introduction to C#
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Introduction to C# and Unity Scripting Basics

Learn why C# is the primary language in Unity and how MonoBehaviour scripts become active components in your scenes. Practice creating a script, attaching it, and observing lifecycle messages in the Console.

In this lesson
C# role • MonoBehaviour • Awake/Start/Update • Attach & Debug
Why C#
C# is a strongly typed, object-oriented language that integrates directly with Unity APIs and the Editor tooling.
MonoBehaviour
Inherit from MonoBehaviour to let Unity call lifecycle methods and attach your script to GameObjects.
Key Takeaway

C# + MonoBehaviour is the bridge between your code and Unity's engine. Use lifecycle methods predictably and debug with Console outputs.

Visual Overview
Script File
Matches class name, contains MonoBehaviour subclass.
GameObject
Attach script as a component to make it run in the scene.
Explore Key Topics
C# role — why it’s used and how it fits the Unity API surface.
Lifecycle methods — Awake, Start, Update: when each runs and why it matters.
Debugging — use Debug.Log to monitor behavior while developing in the Editor.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives frame the practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the role of C# as Unity’s primary scripting language and why it is preferred for gameplay logic. This helps you select the right tools and read Unity A P I references. Second, you will identify the structure of a Unity C# script: the class definition, MonoBehaviour inheritance, and how that gives access to lifecycle methods and components. Third, you will explain the purpose and order of Awake, Start, and Update, and when to use each for initialization, setup, or ongoing updates. Finally, you will create and attach C# scripts to GameObjects and use Debug. Log to observe what your code is doing in the Editor. Each objective pairs a conceptual statement with a short practical check: create a HelloWorldLogger, attach it to a GameObject, and confirm Awake and Start messages appear. As you practice, watch for two common mistakes: mismatched filename and class name, or forgetting to attach the script to an active GameObject. Those checks are simple but essential to getting code running in Unity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Checks
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide focuses on practical checks you will perform to confirm each learning goal. For C# understanding, open the auto-generated script template and point out the using UnityEngine statement and the class header. For script structure, verify the file name matches the class declaration and that the class inherits from MonoBehaviour. For lifecycle order, add Debug. Log messages into Awake, Start, and Update and watch the Console as you enter Play mode to confirm timings. For creation and debugging, attach your script to an empty GameObject and disable or enable that GameObject to see how Start and Awake behave differently. As you run these checks, note a common misconception: Awake does not require the GameObject to be active at editor start, but Start does require the script and GameObject to be enabled to run at the beginning of gameplay. These hands-on checks give immediate feedback and help you avoid trivial errors that block execution. Practice these small experiments to build confidence before moving to larger gameplay scripts.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Practice Checks
Quick verification steps
  1. Open the generated script and confirm the using UnityEngine line and class header exist.
  2. Ensure the filename equals the public class name to avoid compile errors.
  3. Attach the script to an empty GameObject and enable Play to see Start and Awake messages.
  4. Add a Debug.Log inside Update for a live trace, then remove or comment it before shipping to avoid performance issues.
Common misconception
A common mistake is assuming a script in the Project window runs automatically. Only scripts attached to active GameObjects will receive Start and Update calls. Another is changing the file name without updating the class name; Unity will not compile such a script and it will not run.
Tip

When testing, add short, focused Debug.Log messages to confirm order, then remove them when performance matters.

screens.title: C#: Unity's primary scripting language
screens.narratorSegment: C# is an object-oriented, statically typed language that Unity uses to express gameplay logic and Editor scripts. In practical terms, this means you write classes with clearly declared types for variables and methods, and Unity calls those classes when they are attached to GameObjects. The static typing reduces a class of runtime errors and enables the Editor and tooling—like autocompletion and the debugger—to be more effective, which is why professional Unity projects prefer C#. A concrete example: you might declare a public integer to hold health and the type ensures arithmetic and assignment are explicit and predictable. One misconception is that using C# makes development slower; in fact, the language's tooling speeds iteration with reliable compile-time checks and integration with Visual Studio or Rider. Another contrast is that while Unity previously supported other languages, modern Unity development centers on C#, so learning it opens access to the full A P I and community examples. As you progress, remember C# is more than syntax: it's a mindset for organizing game behavior into classes, methods, and well-defined data structures. Try thinking of each GameObject component as a small, single-responsibility class written in C#.

keyIdea.text: C# provides strong typing and Editor support that make writing, debugging, and maintaining gameplay code practical at scale.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › C# in Unity
Definition

C# explained for Unity

C# is the primary language for scripting Unity projects. It gives strong typing, class structure, and good Editor support for game development workflows.

Concrete example
Declare public int health; the type ensures you cannot assign incompatible values accidentally and the Editor shows the field in the Inspector for quick tuning.
Common misconception
Some think C# is harder than scripting alternatives. In Unity, its tooling and typing often make development faster and safer.
Key Takeaway

Treat C# as the language that connects your game rules to Unity’s runtime and Editor support.

Why it matters

Strong typing and Editor integration reduce guesswork and help you iterate quickly on gameplay features.

Tooling

Editors like Visual Studio gain autocompletion, compile-time errors, and debugging because of C#'s structure.

Practice prompt

Open a new C# script and identify the using statement and class header that form the starting point for behavior code.

screens.title: MonoBehaviour and Script Components
screens.narratorSegment: MonoBehaviour is the base class Unity expects for scripts that will be attached to GameObjects and participate in the engine's event loop. Inheriting from MonoBehaviour is not a syntactic nicety — it grants your class access to lifecycle callbacks, the ability to call GetComponent, and to appear as an editable component in the Inspector. A concrete example: public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour is the line that tells Unity to treat that class as a component. A common misconception is to write plain classes and expect them to run; a plain class in the Project folder will not receive Start or Update calls until it is attached through a MonoBehaviour wrapper or used by another active component. In practice you often use plain classes for data containers or pure logic, and MonoBehaviour for things that must integrate with GameObjects, physics, or rendering. Why it matters: understanding what belongs in a MonoBehaviour versus a helper class prevents performance problems and keeps your code modular. Think of MonoBehaviour as the component glue that connects your code to Unity's engine lifecycle. MonoBehaviour and Script Components means only monobehaviour subclasses run as scene components. use plain classes for off-engine logic and monobehaviour for behavior tied to gameobjects.. In practical terms, how inheritance makes scripts attachable components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › MonoBehaviour
Architecture

Scripts as components

When your class inherits MonoBehaviour, Unity lets you attach it to a GameObject and calls lifecycle methods automatically. It also exposes public fields to the Inspector for tuning.

Concrete example
public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour — this single line turns your class into a component Unity can manage in the scene.
Common mistake

Placing gameplay logic in a plain class and expecting Unity to call Start or Update. Only MonoBehaviour receives those callbacks automatically.

Inspector integration

Public fields in a MonoBehaviour are shown in the Inspector so designers can tune values without code changes.

When to use plain classes

Use plain classes for pure data models or utility logic that does not need engine callbacks; this keeps MonoBehaviours focused and efficient.

Check your understanding

If a class must react every frame or access components via GetComponent, it belongs on a GameObject and should inherit MonoBehaviour.

screens.title: Script file and class name matching
screens.narratorSegment: Unity requires that the public class name declared in a C# script matches the script filename. This rule exists because Unity compiles scripts and maps compiled classes back to asset files in the Editor. If the names do not match, Unity cannot link the file to the expected MonoBehaviour type and the script will fail to compile or will not attach properly, producing errors in the Console. A practical example: if your file is HelloWorldLogger. cs the public class inside must be declared public class HelloWorldLogger. A common beginner mistake is renaming the file in the file system or the Editor and forgetting to update the class name, which results in a compile-time mismatch. The fix is simple: either rename the class to match the file or rename the file in the Editor to match the class. This rule helps the engine and tools keep a clear mapping between assets, serialized components in scenes, and runtime types. Always perform a quick compile check after renaming so you catch mismatches early. Script file and class name matching means keep the public class name identical to the script filename to ensure unity compiles and attaches your monobehaviour correctly.. In practical terms, why filename and class name must match in unity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Filename & Class
Rule

Filename must match public class name

This mapping allows Unity to resolve serialized components and compile scripts predictably. A mismatch causes compile errors or missing components at runtime.

Concrete example
If the file is HelloWorldLogger.cs then the script must declare public class HelloWorldLogger to compile and attach properly.
Error symptom

You will see compile errors in the Console or the script will not appear as a selectable component in the Inspector. Fix the name mismatch to resolve the issue.

Quick fix

Rename either the file in the Editor or the public class inside the file so both match exactly, including capitalization.

Check

After renaming, let Unity recompile and verify there are no Console errors that reference class or filename mismatches.

screens.title: Unity lifecycle overview: Awake, Start, Update
screens.narratorSegment: Unity calls a set of lifecycle callbacks in a predictable order that governs initialization and runtime behavior. Awake runs when the script instance is being loaded and is useful for early initialization that must happen even if the GameObject later becomes disabled. Start runs once just before the first frame for an enabled script and is ideal for setup that depends on other objects already initialized. Update runs every frame and is designed for continuous logic like reading input or moving characters. A concrete example: use Awake to cache references via GetComponent so you avoid costly searches later; use Start to initialize values that rely on other components being present; use Update to poll for player input and move the character. A common misconception is thinking Awake and Start are interchangeable; they are ordered and have different guarantees about timing and active state. A short process checklist helps: 1) Awake for fast, early reference setup; 2) Start for one-time runtime setup; 3) Update for per-frame operations. Understanding this order reduces initialization bugs and race conditions. Unity lifecycle overview: Awake, Start, Update means awake initializes on load, start configures when active, and update executes every frame. use each intentionally to avoid timing bugs.. In practical terms, when unity calls these methods and what to do in each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Lifecycle Overview
Process

Awake → Start → Update

Awake()
Called when the instance is loaded. Use this to cache references and set up internal state that other objects may rely on later.
Start()
Called once before the first frame if the script is enabled. Use this for setup that depends on other components being initialized.
Update()
Called every frame. Use for input handling, continuous checks, and frame-dependent behavior.
Concrete example
Use Awake to store a reference to a Rigidbody, Start to set initial velocity based on other objects, and Update to read player input and call Move.
Misconception check
Awake will run even if the GameObject is disabled at load; Start only runs if the component and GameObject are enabled at runtime. They are not interchangeable.
Key Takeaway

Choose Awake for reliable early setup, Start for enabled initialization, and Update for frame-by-frame logic to avoid race conditions.

screens.title: Awake(): Early initialization guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: Awake is called when the script instance is being loaded, and it runs even if the GameObject is later disabled. That makes Awake the right place to perform low-level initialization that must exist before other objects' Start methods run. For example, if you need to cache a commonly used component reference—such as a Rigidbody or AudioSource—call GetComponent in Awake and store the result for later use. One concrete pattern: in Awake you can set private references and internal state so that other components can safely access them during their Start. A common misconception is performing heavy work in Awake that should instead wait until Start or asynchronous systems; prefer quick, deterministic initializations. Another pitfall is relying on other GameObjects being fully initialized in Awake; they may not have executed their Awake or Start yet, so avoid cross-object assumptions. If you need to coordinate initialization order between objects, consider explicit setup methods called from a manager or use script execution order settings. Ultimately, use Awake for reliable, fast, and local setup that prepares your component for the rest of the lifecycle.

keyIdea.text: Use Awake to cache references and set simple internal state. Avoid heavy or order-dependent work there.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Awake()
Definition

Awake: load-time initialization

Called when the instance is loaded; runs regardless of the GameObject's enabled state. Use it to cache components and set quick internal state.

Concrete example
In Awake call GetComponent<Rigidbody> and store the result in a private field so Update can use it without searching each frame.
When not to use Awake
Avoid expensive computations, network calls, or heavy allocations in Awake that could slow scene loading. Reserve those for managed initialization sequences.
Coordination tip
If multiple objects must initialize in a known order, use a manager that calls explicit setup methods after Awake has completed on all objects.
Key Takeaway

Awake is your reliable time to cache references and prepare a component for later Start and Update work.

screens.title: Start(): One-time runtime setup
screens.narratorSegment: Start is called once just before the first frame update for a script instance that is enabled. It is the right place for initialization that depends on other GameObjects or components being present and enabled. For example, if your component needs to read a value calculated by another component or initialize a reference that relies on that other component’s Awake, put that code in Start so the other object has had a chance to set up. A concrete example: you might set the player's initial health value based on values loaded into a GameManager component; perform that assignment in Start so the GameManager is already initialized. A common misconception is treating Start as synchronous across all objects; while Start runs once per enabled script, the ordering between independent objects' Start calls is not guaranteed. If you need specific ordering, use explicit initialization calls or Unity's Script Execution Order. Finally, remember Start only runs if the component and GameObject are active at runtime; disabling the GameObject prevents Start from executing until re-enabled, which is useful for lazy activation patterns. Start(): One-time runtime setup means use start for one-time setup dependent on other components. it runs only for enabled scripts and helps avoid initialization race conditions.. In practical terms, using start for initialization that depends on other components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Start()
Definition

Start: enabled one-time setup

Called once before the first frame for an enabled script. Use it for initialization that relies on other components or scene state.

Concrete example
Set the initial UI text by reading from a GameManager that prepares localized strings in its Awake; perform this in Start so the GameManager is ready.
Activation behavior
If the component or GameObject is disabled at startup, Start will not run until it is enabled. This lets you defer setup until activation.
Ordering caution
Do not assume Start across unrelated objects runs in a predictable order. Use explicit calls or execution-order settings for dependencies.
Key Takeaway

Start is your reliable hook for setup that needs the scene and other components to be ready and enabled.

screens.title: Update(): Per-frame work and performance cautions

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Update()
Definition

Update: the per-frame hook

Called every frame. Best for input handling, animations, and small per-frame updates that are cheap and predictable.

Concrete example
Read Input and apply movement: check input axes and call transform.Translate or a controller method inside Update.
Performance caution
Avoid calling GameObject.Find or allocating new objects inside Update. Cache references and reuse objects to prevent frame drops and garbage collection spikes.
Alternatives
Use FixedUpdate for physics and LateUpdate for camera follow logic. Use coroutines for operations that can run over time without every-frame checks.
Throttle pattern
If a check can be less frequent, measure elapsed time and run it every N seconds instead of each frame to reduce load.
Key Takeaway

Keep Update minimal, cache everything you need, and move expensive logic out of the per-frame loop.

Simple logging pattern

using UnityEngine;
public class HelloWorldLogger : MonoBehaviour
{
void Awake()
{
Debug.Log("HelloWorldLogger: Script is awake and ready!");
}
void Start()
{

}
}

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to the practical introduction to C# in Unity. In this lesson you will learn why C# is the standard language for Unity scripting, how Unity uses classes that inherit from MonoBehaviour to run game behavior, and the basic lifecycle events that determine when your code executes. You will see a small set of essential patterns: creating a C# script file, matching the class name to the filename, attaching that script as a component to a GameObject, and using the print-style Debug. Log function to observe runtime behavior in the Unity Console. Understanding these ideas early saves time when you begin building interactions like player movement, simple AI, or UI responses. A concrete example you will practice is making a Hello World logger that prints messages when the script wakes and when the game starts. Along the way we will highlight two common pitfalls: mismatched filenames and unattached scripts, and the performance cost of logging every frame. By the end of this chapter you will know how to get a simple script running in the Editor and how to reason about what runs when. Ready to begin exploring the core topics and hands-on steps that follow?

These objectives frame the practical skills you will practice. First, you will understand the role of C# as Unity’s primary scripting language and why it is preferred for gameplay logic. This helps you select the right tools and read Unity A P I references. Second, you will identify the structure of a Unity C# script: the class definition, MonoBehaviour inheritance, and how that gives access to lifecycle methods and components. Third, you will explain the purpose and order of Awake, Start, and Update, and when to use each for initialization, setup, or ongoing updates. Finally, you will create and attach C# scripts to GameObjects and use Debug. Log to observe what your code is doing in the Editor. Each objective pairs a conceptual statement with a short practical check: create a HelloWorldLogger, attach it to a GameObject, and confirm Awake and Start messages appear. As you practice, watch for two common mistakes: mismatched filename and class name, or forgetting to attach the script to an active GameObject. Those checks are simple but essential to getting code running in Unity.

This second objectives slide focuses on practical checks you will perform to confirm each learning goal. For C# understanding, open the auto-generated script template and point out the using UnityEngine statement and the class header. For script structure, verify the file name matches the class declaration and that the class inherits from MonoBehaviour. For lifecycle order, add Debug. Log messages into Awake, Start, and Update and watch the Console as you enter Play mode to confirm timings. For creation and debugging, attach your script to an empty GameObject and disable or enable that GameObject to see how Start and Awake behave differently. As you run these checks, note a common misconception: Awake does not require the GameObject to be active at editor start, but Start does require the script and GameObject to be enabled to run at the beginning of gameplay. These hands-on checks give immediate feedback and help you avoid trivial errors that block execution. Practice these small experiments to build confidence before moving to larger gameplay scripts.

C# is an object-oriented, statically typed language that Unity uses to express gameplay logic and Editor scripts. In practical terms, this means you write classes with clearly declared types for variables and methods, and Unity calls those classes when they are attached to GameObjects. The static typing reduces a class of runtime errors and enables the Editor and tooling—like autocompletion and the debugger—to be more effective, which is why professional Unity projects prefer C#. A concrete example: you might declare a public integer to hold health and the type ensures arithmetic and assignment are explicit and predictable. One misconception is that using C# makes development slower; in fact, the language's tooling speeds iteration with reliable compile-time checks and integration with Visual Studio or Rider. Another contrast is that while Unity previously supported other languages, modern Unity development centers on C#, so learning it opens access to the full A P I and community examples. As you progress, remember C# is more than syntax: it's a mindset for organizing game behavior into classes, methods, and well-defined data structures. Try thinking of each GameObject component as a small, single-responsibility class written in C#.

MonoBehaviour is the base class Unity expects for scripts that will be attached to GameObjects and participate in the engine's event loop. Inheriting from MonoBehaviour is not a syntactic nicety — it grants your class access to lifecycle callbacks, the ability to call GetComponent, and to appear as an editable component in the Inspector. A concrete example: public class MyFirstScript : MonoBehaviour is the line that tells Unity to treat that class as a component. A common misconception is to write plain classes and expect them to run; a plain class in the Project folder will not receive Start or Update calls until it is attached through a MonoBehaviour wrapper or used by another active component. In practice you often use plain classes for data containers or pure logic, and MonoBehaviour for things that must integrate with GameObjects, physics, or rendering. Why it matters: understanding what belongs in a MonoBehaviour versus a helper class prevents performance problems and keeps your code modular. Think of MonoBehaviour as the component glue that connects your code to Unity's engine lifecycle. MonoBehaviour and Script Components means only monobehaviour subclasses run as scene components. use plain classes for off-engine logic and monobehaviour for behavior tied to gameobjects.. In practical terms, how inheritance makes scripts attachable components. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unity requires that the public class name declared in a C# script matches the script filename. This rule exists because Unity compiles scripts and maps compiled classes back to asset files in the Editor. If the names do not match, Unity cannot link the file to the expected MonoBehaviour type and the script will fail to compile or will not attach properly, producing errors in the Console. A practical example: if your file is HelloWorldLogger. cs the public class inside must be declared public class HelloWorldLogger. A common beginner mistake is renaming the file in the file system or the Editor and forgetting to update the class name, which results in a compile-time mismatch. The fix is simple: either rename the class to match the file or rename the file in the Editor to match the class. This rule helps the engine and tools keep a clear mapping between assets, serialized components in scenes, and runtime types. Always perform a quick compile check after renaming so you catch mismatches early. Script file and class name matching means keep the public class name identical to the script filename to ensure unity compiles and attaches your monobehaviour correctly.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Unity calls a set of lifecycle callbacks in a predictable order that governs initialization and runtime behavior. Awake runs when the script instance is being loaded and is useful for early initialization that must happen even if the GameObject later becomes disabled. Start runs once just before the first frame for an enabled script and is ideal for setup that depends on other objects already initialized. Update runs every frame and is designed for continuous logic like reading input or moving characters. A concrete example: use Awake to cache references via GetComponent so you avoid costly searches later; use Start to initialize values that rely on other components being present; use Update to poll for player input and move the character. A common misconception is thinking Awake and Start are interchangeable; they are ordered and have different guarantees about timing and active state. A short process checklist helps: 1) Awake for fast, early reference setup; 2) Start for one-time runtime setup; 3) Update for per-frame operations. Understanding this order reduces initialization bugs and race conditions. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Awake is called when the script instance is being loaded, and it runs even if the GameObject is later disabled. That makes Awake the right place to perform low-level initialization that must exist before other objects' Start methods run. For example, if you need to cache a commonly used component reference—such as a Rigidbody or AudioSource—call GetComponent in Awake and store the result for later use. One concrete pattern: in Awake you can set private references and internal state so that other components can safely access them during their Start. A common misconception is performing heavy work in Awake that should instead wait until Start or asynchronous systems; prefer quick, deterministic initializations. Another pitfall is relying on other GameObjects being fully initialized in Awake; they may not have executed their Awake or Start yet, so avoid cross-object assumptions. If you need to coordinate initialization order between objects, consider explicit setup methods called from a manager or use script execution order settings. Ultimately, use Awake for reliable, fast, and local setup that prepares your component for the rest of the lifecycle.

Start is called once just before the first frame update for a script instance that is enabled. It is the right place for initialization that depends on other GameObjects or components being present and enabled. For example, if your component needs to read a value calculated by another component or initialize a reference that relies on that other component’s Awake, put that code in Start so the other object has had a chance to set up. A concrete example: you might set the player's initial health value based on values loaded into a GameManager component; perform that assignment in Start so the GameManager is already initialized. A common misconception is treating Start as synchronous across all objects; while Start runs once per enabled script, the ordering between independent objects' Start calls is not guaranteed. If you need specific ordering, use explicit initialization calls or Unity's Script Execution Order. Finally, remember Start only runs if the component and GameObject are active at runtime; disabling the GameObject prevents Start from executing until re-enabled, which is useful for lazy activation patterns.
